newsitem.title: USA: Lumber prices sink as interest rates rise.
newsitem.headline: Lumber prices sink as interest rates rise.

text.p: Lumber prices tumbled Wednesday as long-term interest rates jumped, raising fears that higher mortgage rates would hurt the housing industry, one of the biggest users of wood.

In other markets, oil prices retreated again as domestic product inventories rose and Iraq resumed exports under a U.N. oil-for-food plan. Grain prices rose ahead of a government supply and demand report.

The drop in the stock market, coupled with higher mortgage rates, could sap consumer confidence and hurt home sales, which have tailed off in recent months. Last week, the Commerce Department reported single-family home sales fell 8.7 percent in October, the largest decline since March.

"If we are going to have higher interest rates, it's not constructive for home buying and people feel slightly pinched, in terms of net worth," said Curt Cunningham, president of Pacific Futures Trading.
"Part of the home buying has been the paper profits on the stock side of the business providing people with a little better net worth," he said.
Lumber for January delivery fell the $10 daily limit for the second straight day at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, closing at $389.50 for 1,000 board feet.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 70.73 points to 6,402.52, its second big drop in the last four sessions, and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell more than 1-3/4 points, raising its yield to 6.63 percent from 6.49 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Stock and bond investors have been on edge since Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks on Thursday about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
Lumber prices had nearly doubled to $488 per 1,000 feet last month from January levels, causing lumber mills to boost production. Prices have retreated as the housing market started to dip.
"Mills have overstated their order files -- there is plently of prompt wood showing up," Cunningham said.
Oil refiners also took advantage of good margins recently and boosted production of gasoline, heating oil and other products, depressing prices that were already in a tailspin.

Traders have been concerned about tight heating oil supplies heading into the peak winter demand season, but the American Petroleum Institute reported late on Tuesday that inventories of distillate fuels -- heating oil and diesel -- rose more than 2 million barrels to 122 million barrels last week.
Gasoline stocks rose particularly sharply, adding nearly 6 million barrels to stand at almost 195 million barrels.

"We know that many refiners were able to lock in the excellent spreads on offer over the last month or so and they are going to continue to crank out production," said Raoul le Blanc of Energy Security Analysis said.
January crude oil fell $1.04 to $23.38 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange, capping a decline of 9 percent since Friday.
Meanwhile, Iraq exported oil for the first time in six years Wednesday, after receiving United Nations clearance to ease an embargo placed on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
"I think people are recognising that this Iraqi deal is a lot more significant than the market was suggesting last week," said Steve Platt at Dean Witter.

Speculation about exports prompted a rise in soybean meal and wheat prices at the Chicago Board of Trade. Traders also expected the government to trim estimates of soybean supplies in its monthly report on Thursday.
Meanwhile, China was rumoured to have bought up to 150,000 tons of soybean meal.

December soybean meal jumped $3.60 to $231.60 a ton and January soybeans rose 6.5 cents to $6.91-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade. December corn added 1 cent to $2.67-1/2 a bushel while December wheat firmed 5.5 cents to $3.99 a bushel.
